Learning Objectives
Identify the etiologies and patient factors that may cause graft failure.
Review imaging studies and physical examination findings to confirm a torn anterior cruciate
ligament graft.
Review nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for the management of failed anterior
cruciate ligament surgery.
Review the outcomes of management of failed anterior cruciate ligament surgery.

Etiology
Overview

Overview
Given the reported failure rate of 3% to 10% after primary anterior cruciate ligament
(ACL) reconstruction, failure most frequently occurs in young (<25 years) and active male
patients within the first 2 years after primary ACL reconstruction. Failure results from
traumatic events, technical errors, or biologic failure. Numerous anatomic, patient-
related, and technical risk factors must be assessed in each patient with ACL graft failure.
Consequently, various approaches are available for the diagnostic work up and
treatment of patients with a recurrent ACL injury compared with patients with a primary
ACL injury. Ultimately, the goal of management is to improve clinical and functional
outcomes and to avoid multiple failures by identifying, considering, and addressing (if
necessary) existing risk factors.
Timing and Occurrence of Recurrent Instability
Early postoperative recurrent instability (Resource 1).
Insufficient/failed femoral and/or tibial graft fixation
Failed graft incorporation
Postoperative infection with subsequent graft failure
Misplaced femoral and/or tibial tunnel with vertical graft
Delayed postoperative recurrent instability
Recurrent trauma with subsequent graft rupture
Insufficient management of concomitant injuries and/or underlying risk factors (eg, meniscal
insufficiency, rotatory knee instability, limb alignment, posterior tibial slope [PTS])
Delayed postoperative infection with subsequent graft failure
Biologic failure
Malpositioned femoral and/or tibial tunnel with vertical graft
Recurrent instability during daily activities
Graft rupture
Misplaced femoral and/or tibial tunnel with vertical graft


Timing and Occurrence of Recurrent Instability
The timing from primary ACL reconstruction to recurrent instability or failure (early
versus delayed) and the circumstances (daily versus sports activities) that trigger
recurrent instability may provide information about the cause of failure. Therefore,
obtaining a detailed patient history is an essential aspect of failure analysis.
Traumatic Failure

Traumatic Failure
Traumatic graft failure accounts for 30% to 40% of graft failures after ACL reconstruction.
Knee ligament registries and prospective studies have shown that sport-related injuries
are the most common cause of traumatic graft failures (approximately 80%), with
noncontact injury mechanisms being predominant.1
Surgical/Technical Failure


Surgical/Technical Failure
Technical failure accounts for more than 20% of graft failures after ACL reconstruction.
Femoral tunnel malpositioning followed by tibial tunnel malpositioning are the most
frequently observed technical errors. Another modifiable risk factor is the graft type.
Graft type for ACL reconstruction (autograft versus Allograft) influences the clinical
outcome, time from surgical management to return to sports activity, progression of
articular cartilage deterioration, and failure rate.
Femoral Tunnel Placement

Femoral Tunnel Placement
The proximal-distal and anterior-posterior position of the anatomic center of the femoral
ACL insertion is located at approximately 25% of the sagittal diameter (along the
Blumensaat line) and 28% of the height (perpendicular to the Blumensaat line) of the
lateral femoral condyle, measured from the most proximal and anterior aspect of the
lateral femoral condyle, respectively. The most common malposition is a femoral tunnel
that is positioned too distally (shallow) and too anteriorly (high); this is associated with a
vertical orientation of the graft (Figure 1). Therefore, native knee kinematics and
rotatory knee stability are insufficiently restored.

Tibial Tunnel Placement

Tibial Tunnel Placement
The desired anatomic anterior-posterior and medial-lateral center of the tibial ACL
tunnel is located at approximately 43% of the sagittal diameter (measured from anterior)
and 47% of the coronal diameter (measured from medial) of the tibial plateau,
respectively. The angulation of the tibial tunnel should be oriented according to the
inclination of the roof of the intercondylar notch. A tibial tunnel that is placed too

Graft Selection
Higher failure rate with allografts compared with autografts
Higher failure rate with hamstring tendon autografts compared with bone-patellar tendon-
bone and quadriceps tendon autografts
More articular cartilage deterioration with allografts compared with autografts
Poorer patient-reported outcomes with allografts compared with autografts
Longer time to return to sports activity with allografts compared with autografts2-5


Graft Selection
Studies have shown that autografts are superior to allografts; therefore, they are the
preferred graft choice, if available.6,7 Various types of autografts are used for ACL
reconstruction, including hamstring, patellar, quadriceps, and peroneal tendons. No
differences between autograft types with respect to clinical and functional outcomes
have been demonstrated. However, recent studies have shown higher failure rates with
hamstring tendon grafts compared with bone-patellar tendon-bone and quadriceps
tendon autografts.8,9 Because the hamstring tendons act as a dynamic restraint against
varus torque, harvesting of hamstring tendons is not recommended in patients with
concomitant medial collateral ligament injuries. A simple graft harvesting technique, low
donor-site morbidity, and the overall versatility of the quadriceps tendon (partial-versus
full-thickness, tendon-bone graft versus all soft-tissue graft) have made it a popular
choice for ACL reconstruction. However, bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft remains
the most frequently used autograft type for ACL reconstruction in the United States.
Graft Fixation
Preconditioning
Pretensioning
10° to 30° of knee flexion
Reduction of tibiofemoral joint orientation

Graft Fixation
Biomechanical studies investigating the material properties of tendon grafts and the
structural properties of a tendon graft in addition to a fixation device construct have
demonstrated plastic deformation (permanent elongation) after cyclic loading because
of viscoelastic construct properties.10,11 Viscoelasticity is a material property combining
viscous (resistance to deformation) and elastic (ability to return to size and shape after
temporary deformation during load application) characteristics in response to load

7/37

application. Therefore, preconditioning of the graft before fixation and pretensioning of
the graft to 40 to 80 N during fixation are recommended to prevent graft slackening.
Given the anisometric behavior of the ACL (ACL fiber length change occurs throughout
range of motion [ie, the ACL is most taut near full extension and less taught in flexion]),
knee joint orientation during graft fixation is essential. Accordingly, graft fixation is
recommended in approximately 10° to 30° of knee flexion combined with a slight
posteriorly directed force on the proximal tibia and axial tension on the draw sutures to
ensure a reduced, native tibiofemoral joint position.
Concomitant Injuries
Common finding
Rotatory knee instability leads to increased stress on the ACL graft, which leads to an
increased failure rate

Concomitant Injuries
Acute ACL injuries are accompanied by concomitant meniscal injuries and injuries of the
peripheral capsuloligamentous structures in as many as 82% and 39% of patients,
respectively. Loss of medial and lateral meniscal tissue causes increased anterior-
posterior and rotatory knee laxity. In addition, injuries to the peripheral
capsuloligamentous structures may lead to anteromedial, anterolateral, posteromedial,
or posterolateral rotatory knee instability, depending on the damaged structures.
Biomechanical studies have shown increased stress on the ACL graft in patients with
combined injuries, which is supported by clinical studies demonstrating increased failure
rates in patients with a high-grade preoperative pivot shift (ie, rotatory knee
instability).12,13 Therefore, a comprehensive preoperative evaluation is recommended to
assess and address (if necessary) concomitant injuries to minimize the risk of graft
failure.

Rehabilitation/Return to Sports Activity
Criterion-based rehabilitation rather than time based rehabilitation
Pivoting sports are discouraged for as many as 9 to 12 months postoperatively

Rehabilitation/Return to Sports Activity
As evidence on postoperative rehabilitation and return to sports activity improves, a
trend toward a criterion-based rehabilitation protocol rather than a time-based
rehabilitation protocol is increasing. A continuous objective physical assessment,
validated return to sports testing, and an evaluation of neuromuscular and psychologic
readiness determine the progression of a criterion-based rehabilitation protocol.
Biologic healing must be considered and prohibits progression that is too rapid. Return
to pivoting sports activity should be discouraged for as many as 9 to 12 months
postoperatively, lowering the failure rate after ACL reconstruction.
Biologic Failure
Disturbance during graft ligamentization and incorporation
Graft maturation is a complex process triggered by biomechanical and biochemical events

Biologic Failure
The intra-articular environment enables the implanted ACL graft to undergo a cascade of
biomechanically and biochemically driven processes, ultimately leading to graft
incorporation and ligamentization. Disturbances of this complex remodeling and
maturation process, which can be triggered by immunologic, vascular, cellular, or
biomechanical events, generally are defined as biologic failure. Risk factors associated
with biologic graft failure resulting from impaired revascularization include smoking,
drug abuse, and diabetes mellitus. Graft incorporation in the area of the femoral and

highlights the importance of anatomic ACL reconstruction.
Risk Factors Associated With ACL Reconstruction Failure

Risk Factors Associated with ACL Reconstruction Failure
Numerous modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors are associated with graft failure
after ACL reconstruction. Patient age, sex, and preoperative and postoperative activity
levels, as well as the bony morphology of the lower limb and its neuromuscular control
must be considered in evaluating patients with graft failure after ACL reconstruction.
Although bony morphology (ie, coronal and sagittal alignment) may be managed
surgically, physical therapy is the standard of care to improve neuromuscular control
and strengthen ACL agonists (ie, hamstring muscles) and core muscles.
Demographics
Age younger than 20 years at the time of primary ACL reconstruction is associated with a risk
for undergoing revision ACL reconstruction

Demographics
Although female sex is a nonmodifiable risk factor for primary ACL injury, males are
more likely to undergo revision ACL reconstruction. In addition, studies have shown that
patients aged 20 years or younger at the time of primary ACL reconstruction have at
higher risk if they undergo revision ACL reconstruction compared with older
counterparts (>20 years).14,15 A patient’s race has not been shown to be a risk factor for
graft failure.
Activity Level

High activity level at the time of primary ACL reconstruction is a risk factor for ipsilateral graft
failure and contralateral ACL injury.

Activity Level
A patient’s activity level at the time of primary ACL reconstruction has been shown to be
a predictor of graft failure, with higher activity levels associated with an increased rate of
graft failure. According to the Marx Activity Rating Scale, an increase of one point
increases the likelihood of sustaining a graft tear by 11%. A higher activity level at the
time of primary ACL reconstruction also is considered a risk factor for contralateral ACL
injury.
Bony Morphology

Bony Morphology
Coronal and sagittal lower limb alignment has been shown to influence the in situ forces
of the ACL, thereby affecting the rate of failure after ACL reconstruction. Differences in
the bony morphology of the distal femur have been observed between individuals in
whom ACL reconstruction fails versus remains intact.
Limb Alignment

Limb Alignment
Biomechanical studies have demonstrated increased in situ ACL graft forces in patients
with varus and valgus malalignment.16,17 In addition, frontal plane malalignment is
associated with increased tibiofemoral contact pressure and meniscal stress in the
corresponding compartment and increased loads on the opposing capsuloligamentous
structures. Based on the underlying bony deformity (ie, tibial versus femoral deformity),

reconstruction may decrease failure rates and increase long-term knee function.
Posterior Tibial Slope

Posterior Tibial Slope
The mean medial and lateral PTS is reported to be approximately 7° and 5°, respectively.
Biomechanical studies demonstrated a positive correlation between PTS and ACL graft
forces and between PTS and anterior tibial translation.18 In addition, an increased PTS in
patients in whom ACL reconstruction fails versus remains intact has been observed in
clinical studies19 (Figure 3). Therefore, slope-reducing osteotomies (ie, anterior closing
wedge high tibial osteotomy) have elicited interest to prevent increased graft forces and
chronic anterior tibial subluxation. A value of 12° occasionally is considered the
transition point from physiologic to pathologic PTS; however, a certain cutoff value,
above which slope-reducing osteotomies are beneficial, has yet to be determined.

Distal Femur Morphology

Distal Femur Morphology
The ACL graft is hosted in the intercondylar notch, and notch impingement has been
reported as a cause of graft failure. However, anatomic tunnel placement in combination
with an individually sized graft, based on preoperative and intraoperative measurements
of the native ACL insertion sites, facilitates ACL reconstruction without the risk of notch
impingement. Increased lateral femoral condyle offset/depth, leading to a more oval-
shaped condyle, has been reported to be another anatomic risk factor for ACL graft
failure.
Evaluation
Patient History
Common symptoms include pain, effusion, stiffness, recurrent instability, limping, and/or gait
abnormalities.
Patients may describe the sensation that the knee is locking, giving way, and/or unstable.
Timing of symptoms can help determine the cause of failure

Patient History
Common symptoms include pain, stiffness, and instability. Differentiating between these
three symptoms is essential to make an accurate diagnosis. Patients also may report
swelling and changes in gait. The patient’s medical records, including past surgical
procedures, surgical reports, associated ligamentous/meniscal/cartilaginous injuries,
type of graft used, and graft fixation method, must be reviewed. Preinjury activity level
and postoperative activity level should be discussed with the patient, and the SEND FEEDBACK

postoperative rehabilitation protocol should be reviewed. Often, returning to aggressive
activities too soon may be a risk factor for failure. An understanding of the patient’s
expectations regarding lifestyle, postoperative activity level, and return to play timing
should be appreciated.
Stiffness
Most common complication after initial ACL reconstruction is loss of range of motion (11% to
35%)
Patients may report loss of flexion and more commonly extension.

Stiffness
Postoperative stiffness is commonly encountered after ACL reconstructions. Many
patients do not tolerate loss of extension because of its effect on gait mechanics and
return to running activities. This may lead to anterior knee pain because of increased
load across the patellofemoral joint from bent knee positioning. This often is a particular
concern of high-activity individuals, including professional athletes. Stiffness may be
related to primary arthrofibrosis from scar tissue or from secondary causes, such as
prolonged immobilization or improper postoperative rehabilitation, leading to
quadriceps inhibition. Early recognition of infrapatellar contraction syndrome is key to
avoiding complications, such as permanent contracture or patellar malalignment. Timing
of surgical management also may play a role in postoperative stiffness. Surgical
management performed during the acute injury phase before recovery of preoperative
range of motion and gait mechanics may be disadvantageous. Other reasons for
quadriceps inhibition include hemarthrosis, arthrofibrosis, intercondylar notch scarring,
capsulitis, cyclops lesion, nonanatomic placement or overtensioning of the graft,
infection, and complex regional pain syndrome.
Physical Examination


Physical Examination
A thorough physical examination is important to help guide diagnosis and surgical
planning. Inspection of the limb for any previous surgical incisions and scars is
necessary. Evaluate donor-site incisions as well. Ruling out infection is critical because
patients with an infection may require urgent treatment; therefore, evaluate for any skin
changes, drainage from the incision, warmth with palpation, effusion, and abnormal vital
signs. Valgus and varus deformity of the lower extremity can be evaluated with the
patient in a standing position. In addition, gait evaluation may reveal increased internal
rotation during the initial swing phase. Varus or valgus thrust during ambulation may
indicate possible concomitant ligamentous injury. Neuromuscular examination may
reveal decreased muscle tone and strength, especially quadriceps and hamstring
atrophy and weakness. This finding may be related to improper postoperative
rehabilitation. Common peroneal nerve injury is associated with 15% to 29% of
posterolateral corner (PLC) injuries. Patients with a PLC injury may experience ipsilateral
foot numbness and/or weakness with ankle or toe dorsiflexion because of peroneal
nerve injury. Special tests and physical examination maneuvers can help guide imaging
studies and additional surgical management.

Imaging Studies
Should supplement but not replace patient history and physical examination
Useful for preoperative planning

Imaging Studies
After a detailed patient history is obtained and a thorough physical examination is
performed, the next step is to obtain imaging studies that will provide information to
strategically plan the revision procedure. The typical workup includes radiography, CT,
and MRI, which can provide details that will dictate how to approach revision ACL
reconstruction. Imaging studies also can help determine if other procedures are
indicated in addition to revision ACL reconstruction.
Radiography
Plain radiographs
Standing AP view
Lateral view in 30o of knee flexion
Merchant view: axial view in 45o of knee flexion
Fick view: standing PA view in 45o of knee flexion
Standing alignment radiographs (hip to ankle)

Radiography
Radiography often is the first imaging study performed in the clinical setting and can be
helpful in surgical planning. Various fixation methods are available for ACL
reconstruction, and radiographs can provide insight regarding tunnel positioning.
Radiography also is a good preoperative imaging modality to evaluate hardware
placement and reveal any migration or potential interference with revision surgery. Full-
length radiographs can be obtained to assess lower limb alignment and help determine

failure.
Comparison of recent radiographs with previous radiographs also may aid in assessing

Discussing progression of osteoarthritis with the patient may help shape short- and long-

Computed Tomography
Best imaging modality for assessing tunnel widening/enlargement
Consider obtaining three-dimensional reconstruction images if possible

Computed Tomography
CT is the best imaging modality for observing bony morphology in patients in whom ACL
reconstruction fails. CT is most useful for evaluating tunnel widening and bone tunnel
placement. This may help determine if considerable bone loss is present, which may
alter surgical decisions, such as pursuing two-stage revision ACL reconstruction with
interim bone grafting.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Obtain coronal, sagittal, axial, coronal oblique, and sagittal oblique views
Best imaging modality for assessing the integrity of the graft
Can observe any additional meniscus, chondral, or ligamentous injuries and bone bruises

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is a useful imaging modality that provides detailed information regarding graft
preservation, signal intensity, and tunnel preservation. Evaluation for missed meniscal

Although MRI provides great detail, many situations exist in which MRI findings may not

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management of failed ACL reconstruction is reserved for specific circumstances.
Indications
Primary complaint is knee pain
Older than 45 years/sedentary lifestyle
Increased risk associated with surgical management

Indications
If a patient’s primary complaint is knee pain that cannot be attributed to other etiologies
(eg, tunnel enlargement, tunnel malpositioning), nonsurgical management may be
considered because revision ACL reconstruction likely will not alleviate the pain. Older
patients (generally >45 years) in whom ACL reconstruction fails often are treated
nonsurgically. In addition, patients with medical comorbidities that would substantially
increase the risk of adverse events are treated nonsurgically.
Contraindications
Knee instability

Contraindications
If a patient’s main complaint is knee instability, nonsurgical management generally is
avoided.
Techniques/Procedures
Avoiding cutting and pivoting activities
Physical therapy
Functional bracing

Techniques/Procedures
The mainstay of nonsurgical management for failed ACL reconstruction is avoiding
activities that place the knee at risk of instability; this includes activities that involve
cutting and pivoting. Physical therapy often is performed to focus on strengthening the
dynamic stabilizers of the knee to increase stability during normal activities (ie,
hamstring strengthening). Functional bracing also may be used to reduce functional
deficits, provide stability, and prevent injury.
Surgical Management
In general, surgical management of failed ACL reconstruction is performed to restore a stable,
functional knee. Revision ACL reconstruction alone will not manage contributing intra-articular
pathology but may help prevent additional injury to intra-articular structures.
Indications
Persistent knee instability
Return to cutting or pivoting sports

Indications
Surgical management is the typical treatment option for the management of failed ACL
reconstruction, particularly if the patient’s main complaint is persistent knee instability.
Revision ACL reconstruction also is indicated in patients who wish to return to activities
that depend on the ACL, such as cutting and/or pivoting sports activity.
Contraindications
Primary complaint is pain with no imaging abnormality
Functional ACL
Lack of subjective and objective instability
Sedentary lifestyle
Techniques
Single-stage procedure
Two-stage procedure
Two main techniques are available for revision ACL reconstruction: single-stage or two-stage
procedures.
Single-Stage Procedure
Preferred approach
Prior bone tunnels are in an appropriate position without considerable osteolysis/widening
(<15 mm)
Prior bone tunnels are in an inappropriate position with no overlap to anatomic footprints
Malalignment should be managed.
Meniscus deficiency should be considered.

Single-Stage Procedure

A single-stage procedure is the preferred approach for revision ACL reconstruction
because it avoids the morbidity and economic burden associated with an additional
surgical procedure. If the prior bone tunnels are in an appropriate position without
considerable osteolysis/widening (ie, <15 mm), a single-stage procedure is the preferred
treatment option. In addition, the bone must be of good quality, and the previously
placed hardware must not interfere with the revision procedure. Limb alignment must
be carefully evaluated, and any malalignment should be managed during revision ACL
reconstruction. Occasionally, malalignment may preclude a single-stage procedure,
necessitating two-stage revision.
Two-Stage Procedure
Manipulation under anesthesia with arthroscopic lysis of adhesions if range of motion is not
equal to that of the contralateral knee after nonsurgical management
Bone graft tunnels allow for bony healing before second stage if prior bone tunnels are
enlarged or malpositioned (Figure 4)

therapy, splinting, and pharmacotherapy, then manipulation under anesthesia with


Preoperative Planning
After the decision is made to manage failed ACL reconstruction surgically, thorough
preoperative evaluation and planning are essential. Before proceeding with the revision
ACL reconstruction, the surgeon must scrutinize all imaging studies, including
radiographs, MRIs, and CT scans, to determine the appropriate surgical procedure. The
cause of the prior ACL reconstruction failure should be determined and managed at the
time of revision. The surgeon should be prepared to manage all concomitant pathology
observed on preoperative imaging studies, such as meniscal tears, cartilage lesions, or
injuries to other ligamentous structures.

Graft Selection
Grafts can broadly categorized into two groups: autograft and allograft. Graft selection
must account for patient-specific factors. The literature contains mixed results with
respect to autograft versus allograft. Some studies show no difference in outcomes,20
whereas the Multicenter ACL Revision Study Group demonstrated a higher rate of failed
revision ACL reconstruction if allograft was used.21
Allograft
Can use allograft with attached bone block or all soft-tissue allograft
Advantages: expedites procedure, eliminates donor-site morbidity
Disadvantages: increased risk of disease transmission, expensive, incorporation and
recellularization slower, associated with higher failure rate in young patients

Allograft
The use of an allograft expedites the revision procedure and eliminates donor-site
morbidity because no graft harvest takes place. Achilles tendon and bone-patellar
tendon-bone allografts contain large bone blocks, which may be advantageous in filling
bony voids from the previous ACL reconstruction. All soft-tissue allografts, such as
hamstring and tibialis anterior grafts, also may be used. However, the use of allograft
tissue increases the risk of disease transmission, which should be discussed with the
patient preoperatively. Finally, allografts may be expensive and have been shown to
incorporate and recellularize more slowly than autografts.
Autograft
Preferred tissue
Option of bone-patellar tendon-bone, hamstring, quadriceps tendon, and contralateral grafts
Advantages: faster graft healing, decreased risk of late atraumatic knee instability


Autograft
Autograft tissue typically is preferred over allograft because it decreases the time to graft
healing, which may decrease the risk of late atraumatic knee instability. Autograft
options include ipsilateral and contralateral bone-patellar tendon-bone, hamstring, and
quadriceps tendon. If allograft was used for initial ACL reconstruction, then autograft is
preferred to avoid previously undiagnosed graft rejection. The biggest disadvantage of
autograft use is donor-site morbidity, which varies depending on the graft selected.

Supine


Patient Positioning
The patient is placed in the supine position on the surgical table. A nonsterile tourniquet
is applied to the upper thigh, and the leg is placed in an arthroscopic leg holder, which
should allow for hyperflexion of the knee for femoral tunnel preparation. The author of
this lesson prefers to remove the foot of the bed and place the contralateral leg in the
hemilithotomy position.

Single-Stage Procedure
Diagnostic arthroscopy is performed, and the prior ACL graft is débrided. If the tunnels
are in an anatomic position and are not enlarged, then existing hardware is removed. If
the hardware from previous ACL reconstruction will not interfere with single-stage
reconstruction, it should be left in place to prevent additional morbidity. Any additional
intra-articular pathology should be addressed (eg, meniscal tears, cartilage lesions). If
the tunnels from the previous graft are to be completely bypassed, proceed with the
reconstruction technique in the same manner as that for primary ACL reconstruction. If
the previous tunnels are being used, they should be thoroughly débrided and reamed.
The new graft can be passed and secured with the use of an interference screw, with
secondary extra-articular fixation on the femur and tibia, if necessary. If the previous
tunnels are anatomic with good bone quality, then divergent tunnels can be drilled and
reamed. These new tunnels will house the new graft, and bone grafting (allograft dowels)
can be performed in the previous tunnels.

If the surgeon determines that a staged procedure is necessary, the complicating factors are
addressed during the first stage and the ACL is reconstructed during the second stage.
First stage
If considerable preoperative loss of motion is present, then manipulation under anesthesia
and arthroscopic lysis of adhesions and débridement should be performed. After the first
stage, aggressive rehabilitation and physical therapy are necessary to regain motion equal
to that of the contralateral knee.
If the prior femoral and/or tibial tunnels are enlarged more than 15 mm, the bony voids are
filled during the first stage. Diagnostic arthroscopy is performed, and the prior ACL graft is
débrided. The previous tunnels are thoroughly débrided and reamed to remove all sclerotic
bone while preserving as much healthy bone as possible. The tunnels are then packed with
the autograft or allograft. Often, premade allograft bone dowels are used; however, other
allografts can be shaped to fit the tunnel. Allograft bone chips or bone substitutes
(demineralized bone matrix, calcium phosphate) may be used. After the first stage, the
patient is allowed to range the knee to prevent contractures. Imaging studies (radiographs
or preferably CT scans) are obtained after a minimum of 12 weeks to ensure complete graft
incorporation before proceeding with the second stage.
If active joint infection is suspected, the first stage consists of arthroscopic irrigation and
débridement with or without graft and hardware removal. An extended course of antibiotic
agents is then administered, and rehabilitation and physical therapy are performed to
maintain motion. After elimination of active infection is confirmed, the surgeon can
proceed with the second stage. Multiple débridement procedures may be necessary.
Retaining the previous graft often can be accomplished.
Second stage
Before proceeding with the second stage, the surgeon must ensure that all factors
necessitating the first stage have been resolved (eg, stiffness, bony defects, infection). The
second stage is performed in the same manner as that for primary ACL reconstruction.

Lateral Extra-Articular Tenodesis/Anterolateral Ligament
Reconstruction
If the knee is highly unstable, as determined by a high-grade pivot shift, some surgeons
may choose to add extra-articular stability. Two commonly used techniques are lateral
extra-articular tenodesis and anterolateral ligament reconstruction. Lateral extra-
articular tenodesis involves harvesting a strip of iliotibial band, leaving it attached to its
distal insertion on the Gerdy tubercle, and tenodesis of it to the lateral epicondyle.
Anterolateral ligament reconstruction involves the use of allograft tissue as a free graft
on the anterolateral aspect of the knee. Studies investigating these techniques have
demonstrated mixed results.22-25
Osteotomies
Manage severe malalignment
Can be performed during single- or two-stage revision
High tibial osteotomy for varus malalignment and/or slope correction
Distal femoral osteotomy for valgus malalignment

Osteotomies
Osteotomies can performed to manage severe malalignment and can be performed
during single-stage revision ACL reconstruction or as the first stage of two-stage revision.
If a high tibial osteotomy (for varus malalignment) or distal femoral osteotomy (for
valgus malalignment) is performed as part of two-stage revision, then healing of the
osteotomy must be verified before proceeding with ACL reconstruction.

Articular Cartilage Management
Cartilage defects observed on preoperative imaging studies or noted intra-operatively
should be managed to provide the most satisfactory long-term outcomes. Various
techniques may be used, including chondroplasty, microfracture, osteochondral
autograft transplantation, or osteochondral allograft transplantation, depending on the
size of the lesion. If one of these techniques is to be used, the procedure should be
discussed with the patient preoperatively because it may affect postoperative
rehabilitation and weight-bearing status.

Meniscal allograft reconstruction may be considered in patients with high-grade instability and
young patients with (sub)total meniscal deficiency

is thought to have a low likelihood of healing, then a simple partial meniscectomy is
performed. The tear should be repaired if it is in the red-red zone, if the tear involves the

PLC Reconstruction
Unidentified PLC injury is a well-established cause of failed ACL reconstruction. If the PLC
structures are damaged, then PLC reconstruction should be performed to prevent failed
revision reconstruction. This can be performed during single-stage revision ACL
reconstruction or as during the first stage of two-stage revision ACL reconstruction.
Various techniques are available for PLC reconstruction, and the specific technique used
is based on surgeon preference (Resource 2).


Complications
Unfortunately, increased incidence of adverse events and poor outcomes is observed
after revision ACL reconstruction compared with primary ACL reconstruction. However,
the possible adverse outcomes are similar to those that occur after primary ACL
reconstruction. One of the most dreaded complications is failure of the revision ACL
graft. Graft re-rupture rates between 5% and 24% have been reported. If pain was
considered the primary reason for failure of previous ACL reconstruction, then revision
ACL reconstruction may not afford considerable symptomatic relief. Posttraumatic
meniscal and/or chondral changes are another complication; they occur more often
after revision ACL reconstruction compared with primary ACL reconstruction because
additional traumatic events to the knee have occurred. Infection also is a possibility, and
the risk of infection is increased if allografts are used. Other complications include
quadriceps weakness, loss of motion, complex regional pain syndrome, and deep vein
thrombosis.


Rehabilitation
After revision ACL reconstruction, some surgeons recommend postoperative
rehabilitation protocols similar to those for primary ACL reconstruction; other surgeons
recommend more conservative postoperative rehabilitation protocols, considering the
revision knee as a compromised environment because revascularization may take as
long as 6 months. In general, the knee is placed in a hinged knee brace, and the patient
is allowed to range the knee with emphasis placed on early extension; however, flexion
may be limited, depending on the procedures performed. Weight bearing often is
permitted as tolerated; however, it may be limited if deemed necessary based on
concurrent procedures performed. Quadriceps strengthening is performed via a
combination of closed-chain kinetic and isometric exercises under the supervision of a
physical therapist; proprioceptive training also is performed. Straight-line running
typically is initiated at approximately 4 months postoperatively, with sport-specific
activities initiated by 8 to 9 months postoperatively, pending progress. Return to athletic
activity often takes as long as or more than, 1 year.
Outcomes
Outcomes depend on managing the primary etiology of failure
In general, the outcomes of revision ACL reconstruction are inferior to those of primary ACL
reconstruction.


Outcomes
The outcome of revision ACL reconstruction depends on managing the mode of failure
of the previous ACL graft. Typically, the outcomes of revision ACL reconstruction are
inferior to those of primary ACL reconstruction. The objective failure rate after revision
ACL reconstruction may be as high as 14%, which is more than double the rate reported
after primary ACL reconstruction.2 Failures in the Multicenter Orthopaedic Outcomes
Network cohort were 2.9% at 2 years postoperatively and 5.8% at 5 years
postoperatively.2,3 A comparison of single-stage revision ACL reconstruction with
primary ACL reconstructions revealed no considerable differences in objective
International Knee Documentation Committee scores; however, substantially poorer
subjective functional test results and Lysholm scores were reported in the revision
cohort.4 A study prospectively comparing two-stage revision ACL reconstruction with
primary ACL reconstruction reported substantially inferior objective International Knee
Documentation Committee scores, greater range of motion deficits, and crepitus in the
two-stage revision cohort.5 Similarly, studies comparing revision versus primary ACL
reconstruction have reported inferior Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Scores
and Lysholm scores, greater pivot shift, greater reduction in Tegner Activity Scale scores,
decreased muscle strength, and increased radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis in the
revision cohort.2,26 Another study reported that 68% of patients who underwent revision
ACL reconstruction were able to return to their preoperative activity level compared with
75% to 85% of patients who underwent primary ACL reconstruction.27
